questions.q: Why is hallucination described in this lesson as a predictable consequence of the model's mechanism, not a separate bug?
options: Because the model's objective is to generate plausible next tokens, with no built-in check for whether the result is actually true
Because hallucination only happens due to random hardware errors
Because the model intentionally lies to users
Because hallucination was deliberately programmed as a feature
questions.explain: Next-token prediction optimizes for plausibility given learned patterns, not for truth — when probable and true diverge, confident but false output is the predictable result.

questions.q: Which condition from the lesson increases the likelihood of hallucination?
options: Asking a precise question about a well-documented, widely discussed topic
Using a very short prompt with no follow-up questions
Asking for a precise citation or statistic on a topic the model has thin training coverage of
Asking the model to repeat a sentence verbatim
questions.explain: Specificity without grounding — like an exact citation on a niche topic — pushes the model to generate from a general pattern rather than a memorized fact, increasing hallucination risk.

questions.q: Why can a long, multi-step generation make hallucination worse?
options: Longer generations always use a different, less accurate model
The context window resets automatically partway through long responses
An early small error becomes permanent context for every token generated after it, and can compound
Long generations are never autoregressive
questions.explain: Because generation is autoregressive, an early mistake becomes fixed context for everything that follows, giving it room to compound into a larger error later in the same response.

questions.q: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) do to reduce hallucination?
options: It deletes the model's training data
It forces the model to always use greedy decoding
It increases the model's temperature to maximum
It grounds answers in real, retrieved source text instead of relying purely on what the model memorized
questions.explain: RAG retrieves real, relevant source text and feeds it into the prompt, giving the model something grounded to draw from instead of relying purely on memorized patterns.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the only fully reliable backstop for high-stakes LLM output today?
options: Increasing the temperature parameter
Human review
Using the smallest available model
Disabling retrieval-augmented generation
questions.explain: No current technique eliminates hallucination completely; for legal, medical, financial, or other high-stakes output, human review remains the only fully reliable backstop.
